analogy.p: Think of electrons as coins. In a displacement reaction, a magnesium atom is a person who hands over two coins (**oxidation**, loss of electrons) and a copper ion is a person who accepts the two coins (**reduction**, gain of electrons). The coins never vanish: the total number stays the same, which is why oxidation and reduction always occur together. The analogy breaks down because real electrons are all identical and are not 'owned' by particular atoms permanently, and the transfer is not a deliberate act - it happens because magnesium holds its outer electrons less strongly than copper does.

bullets: **Oxidation = gain of oxygen** (e.g. magnesium burning: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO, the magnesium gains oxygen so it is oxidised).
**Reduction = loss of oxygen** (e.g. copper(II) oxide heated in hydrogen: CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O, the copper oxide loses oxygen so it is reduced).
**Oxidation = loss of electrons** and **reduction = gain of electrons** (Higher tier). Memory aid: **OIL RIG** - Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).
The two definitions agree: when magnesium gains oxygen it forms Mg2+ by losing two electrons, so it is oxidised by both definitions.
If a question just says 'oxidised' with an equation containing oxygen, use the oxygen definition; if it mentions ions, electrons or half equations, use the electron definition.
The words always come as a pair: whenever something is oxidised, something else is reduced in the same reaction.
core.h: The two definitions you must know
core.p: Chemists use two definitions of oxidation and reduction, and the exam board expects you to use whichever the question context suggests. The older, simpler idea is about **oxygen**: **oxidation is gain of oxygen** and **reduction is loss of oxygen**. The more powerful idea (Higher tier) is about **electrons**: **oxidation is loss of electrons** and **reduction is gain of electrons**. The second definition works for every reaction, including ones that contain no oxygen at all, which is why it is the one used for ions, displacement and electrolysis.

bullets: In CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O: copper oxide loses oxygen (**reduced**) while hydrogen gains oxygen (**oxidised**).
In Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2: iron(III) oxide is **reduced** to iron; carbon monoxide is **oxidised** to carbon dioxide.
The substance that is oxidised is called the **reducing agent** because it causes the other substance to be reduced (e.g. carbon monoxide, hydrogen, carbon).
The substance that is reduced is the **oxidising agent** because it causes the other to be oxidised (e.g. oxygen, copper(II) oxide).
Total electrons lost by the oxidised species always equals total electrons gained by the reduced species.
Not every reaction is redox: neutralisation (H+ + OH- → H2O) and precipitation involve no electron transfer at all.
core.h: Redox: oxidation and reduction happen together
core.p: A reaction in which both oxidation and reduction occur is called a **redox reaction** (reduction-oxidation). The reason they must be paired is conservation: electrons cannot just disappear or appear, so if one species loses electrons another has to gain exactly the same number. In the same way, when oxygen is lost from one substance it has to be transferred to another substance. This is why you can always point to two partners in a redox equation: the one that is oxidised and the one that is reduced.

bullets: Magnesium: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO (bright white flame, white powder). Magnesium is **oxidised**.
Iron: 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3 (the chemistry behind rusting, which also needs water). Iron is **oxidised**.
Copper: 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO (the surface of heated copper goes black). Copper is **oxidised**.
Methane burning: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. Carbon and hydrogen in the fuel gain oxygen so the fuel is **oxidised** (complete combustion).
Hydrogen burning: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Hydrogen is **oxidised**; the oxygen is reduced as an oxygen molecule ends up as O2- ions in a compound (electron view).
Because oxygen is the oxidising agent in all of these, any reaction of a substance with oxygen is classed as oxidation.
core.h: Oxidation by gain of oxygen: burning and rusting
core.p: Many everyday reactions are oxidations in the oxygen sense. When a metal burns in air it joins with oxygen to form a metal oxide, and when a fuel burns it joins with oxygen to form oxides such as carbon dioxide and water. Rusting is a slower oxidation of iron, needing both oxygen and water, which forms hydrated iron(III) oxide. These examples let you spot oxidation quickly in an exam: look for the formula of the substance gaining an O.

bullets: Iron(III) oxide in the blast furnace: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2. Iron oxide is **reduced**; carbon monoxide is **oxidised**.
Zinc oxide heated with carbon: ZnO + C → Zn + CO. Zinc oxide is **reduced**; carbon is **oxidised**.
Copper(II) oxide heated with hydrogen: CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O. A black solid turns pink-brown as the oxide is **reduced** to copper.

Carbon can reduce oxides of metals **less reactive than carbon** (zinc, iron, copper). Metals **more reactive than carbon** (potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium) must be extracted by **electrolysis** of their molten compounds.
Electrolysis is also reduction: the metal ions gain electrons at the cathode (e.g. Al3+ + 3e- → Al).
Link to other topics: this is why extraction of aluminium needs huge amounts of electrical energy while iron can be made in a blast furnace.
core.h: Reduction by loss of oxygen: extracting metals
core.p: Reduction in the oxygen sense is what happens when a metal ore (usually an oxide) is turned into the metal. The metal oxide loses its oxygen to another substance that is a better 'oxygen acceptor', most commonly carbon or carbon monoxide. This is only possible when the metal is less reactive than carbon, because a more reactive metal holds on to oxygen more strongly than carbon can pull it away. This is the core idea behind the choice of extraction method.

bullets: Magnesium atom to ion: Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-. Electrons are on the **right**, so this is **oxidation** (loss).
Copper ion to atom: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu. Electrons are on the **left**, so this is **reduction** (gain).
Chlorine molecule to chloride ions: Cl2 + 2e- → 2Cl-. Chlorine **gains** electrons so it is **reduced**.
Oxygen forming oxide ions: O2 + 4e- → 2O2-. Oxygen is **reduced** even though it is the 'oxidising agent' - an easy confusion to avoid.
Rule of thumb for half equations: electrons on the left means reduction; electrons on the right means oxidation.
Metals form positive ions by oxidation; the more easily a metal loses electrons, the more reactive it is.
core.h: Redox in terms of electrons (Higher tier)
core.p: At Higher tier you must describe oxidation and reduction as **electron transfer**. A metal atom becomes a positive ion by **losing** electrons, so metals are always **oxidised** when they form ions. A non-metal atom becomes a negative ion by **gaining** electrons, so it is **reduced**. A positive ion can also be reduced when it gains electrons and turns back into an atom. The charge on the ion tells you how many electrons moved, which is what makes balancing half equations possible.

bullets: Word equation: magnesium + copper sulfate → magnesium sulfate + copper. Symbol equation: Mg + CuSO4 → MgSO4 + Cu.
Ionic equation: **Mg + Cu2+ → Mg2+ + Cu**. The sulfate ion SO4 2- appears unchanged on both sides, so it is a **spectator ion** and is left out.
Half equations: **Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-** (oxidation) and **Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu** (reduction). Add them and cancel the 2e- to get the ionic equation.
Observation: blue solution fades as Cu2+ is used up, a pink-brown solid (copper) forms, and the temperature rises.
Silver nitrate with copper: Cu + 2Ag+ → Cu2+ + 2Ag. Copper is oxidised and silver ions reduced; the solution turns blue as Cu2+ forms.
No reaction occurs if the metal is less reactive than the metal in the salt, e.g. copper metal with magnesium sulfate solution.
core.p: A more reactive metal will **displace** a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt. In electron terms, the more reactive metal atoms lose electrons (are oxidised) and the less reactive metal ions gain those electrons (are reduced). You can see the reaction happen: a coating of the less reactive metal appears, the solution may change colour, and the temperature often rises because the reaction is exothermic. Writing the **ionic equation** removes the spectator ions and shows the electron transfer clearly.

bullets: Word equation: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2.
Ionic equation: **Mg + 2H+ → Mg2+ + H2**. The chloride ions are spectators.
Half equations: Mg → Mg2+ + 2e- (**oxidation**) and 2H+ + 2e- → H2 (**reduction**).
Iron with sulfuric acid: Fe + H2SO4 → FeSO4 + H2; ionic Fe + 2H+ → Fe2+ + H2 (iron is oxidised to iron(II)).
The test for hydrogen is a lit splint, which gives a **squeaky pop**.
Copper, silver and gold do not react with dilute acids because they are below hydrogen and cannot reduce H+.
core.p: When a metal reacts with a dilute acid such as hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, it forms a salt and hydrogen gas. The hydrogen comes from the hydrogen ions (H+) in the acid. In electron terms, the metal atoms lose electrons and the hydrogen ions gain them, so the metal is oxidised and the hydrogen ions are reduced. Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series can do this, because they are able to give electrons to H+ ions.

bullets: Order (most to least reactive): potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper.
A metal will displace any metal **below** it from a solution of its salt, and from its oxide when heated.
Metals above hydrogen react with dilute acid; metals below it do not.
The more reactive the metal, the more easily it is **oxidised** and the more stable its compounds are (the harder to reduce them).

Thermite reaction: 2Al + Fe2O3 → Al2O3 + 2Fe. Aluminium (more reactive) takes the oxygen from iron oxide; iron oxide is reduced and aluminium oxidised, releasing a lot of heat - used to weld railway lines.
Link to rates: reactivity is judged by how vigorously bubbles form with acid, or how quickly the metal reacts with water.
core.h: Reactivity series and tendency to lose electrons
core.p: The reactivity series ranks metals by how readily they react, and the deeper idea is that it ranks them by how readily they **lose electrons to form positive ions** (how easily they are oxidised). Potassium loses its outer electron very easily, so it is violently reactive; copper holds its electrons more strongly, so it is unreactive. Carbon and hydrogen are placed in the series for comparison because they are used to reduce oxides and because acids contain hydrogen ions. Knowing this lets you predict displacement, acid and extraction results.

bullets: Molten lead(II) bromide: at the cathode Pb2+ + 2e- → Pb (**reduction**).
At the anode: 2Br- → Br2 + 2e- (**oxidation**); bromine vapour is seen.
Molten aluminium oxide dissolved in cryolite: Al3+ + 3e- → Al at the cathode; 2O2- → O2 + 4e- at the anode.
The oxygen produced at the carbon anode reacts with the carbon: C + O2 → CO2, so the anodes burn away and must be replaced regularly.
In half equations the electrons must balance in the overall process: the number lost at the anode equals the number gained at the cathode.
Link to extraction: electrolysis is a reduction method for reactive metals that carbon cannot reduce.
core.h: Oxidation and reduction in electrolysis (Higher tier)
core.p: In electrolysis, the ionic compound is melted or dissolved so the ions can move, and electricity makes the ions discharge at the electrodes. **Positive ions move to the negative electrode (cathode)** and gain electrons, which is **reduction**. **Negative ions move to the positive electrode (anode)** and lose electrons, which is **oxidation**. A helpful phrase is that **reduction occurs at the cathode, oxidation at the anode** (many students use 'RedCat, AnOx').

bullets: Step 1: write the formula of the species and the ion (Zn → Zn2+).
Step 2: balance the charge by adding electrons (Zn → Zn2+ + 2e-): 0 = 2+ + 2(-) = 0.
Step 3: for reductions, add electrons to the positive side (Ag+ + e- → Ag).
Step 4: to combine, equalise electrons: Zn → Zn2+ + 2e- and 2Ag+ + 2e- → 2Ag give Zn + 2Ag+ → Zn2+ + 2Ag.
State symbols can be added: Zn(s) + 2Ag+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + 2Ag(s).
Always check atoms and charge balance on both sides before you finish.
core.p: A half equation shows just one half of a redox process: the oxidation or the reduction on its own. To write one, start with the species and the ion it becomes, balance the atoms, then add electrons to balance the **charge**. Check that the total charge on both sides is equal. When you combine two half equations into an overall ionic equation, multiply them so the number of electrons matches and then cancel the electrons.

bullets: Cl2 + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br2; ionic Cl2 + 2Br- → 2Cl- + Br2.
Half equations: Cl2 + 2e- → 2Cl- (chlorine **reduced**) and 2Br- → Br2 + 2e- (bromide **oxidised**).
Observation: colourless bromide solution turns orange/brown as bromine forms.
Chlorine with potassium iodide gives a brown solution of iodine.
Bromine does not displace chlorine from chloride, as chlorine is more reactive.
This shows that for non-metals, the more reactive element is the one that gains electrons more easily.
core.h: Halogen displacement as redox (Higher tier link)
core.p: The same electron ideas explain the displacement of halogens in Group 7. A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt, because the more reactive halogen atom gains electrons more readily. The halide ion that is displaced loses electrons to become the free halogen. Reactivity falls going down the group, so chlorine can displace bromine and iodine, bromine can displace iodine, but not the reverse.

bullets: Rusting: iron is oxidised in the presence of water and oxygen to form hydrated iron(III) oxide.
Hydrogen fuel cell: hydrogen is oxidised and oxygen is reduced, producing water and a voltage (link to energy changes).
Respiration: glucose is oxidised (gain of oxygen) to carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy.
Sacrificial protection: a more reactive metal (e.g. zinc) is oxidised in preference to the iron, so the iron is protected.
Cells and batteries: the more reactive metal in a cell is oxidised and the electrons flow through the circuit.
Combustion of fuels (complete and incomplete) are oxidations; incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide or carbon as less oxygen is gained.
core.h: Other examples and applications of redox
core.p: Redox reactions are everywhere, which is why this topic links so many others. Corrosion, batteries, fuel cells, extraction, bleaching and respiration all depend on electron transfer. You do not need all the details, but recognising these as oxidation and reduction can help you answer unfamiliar-context questions. In unfamiliar questions, always find which substance gains oxygen or loses electrons first, then name the process.

exam: **Define** (1 mark): 'Oxidation is the loss of electrons' or 'gain of oxygen'; 'reduction is the gain of electrons' or 'loss of oxygen'. Match the definition to the context in the question.
**Identify the substance oxidised/reduced** (1-2 marks): name the species and give a reason, e.g. 'Iron oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen'. A reason is usually needed for the mark.

**Explain in terms of electrons** (2-3 marks): say which species loses electrons, which gains, and link them: 'Magnesium atoms lose 2 electrons (oxidation) which are gained by copper ions (reduction)'.
**Write an ionic equation** (2 marks): remove spectator ions, balance atoms and charge. One mark for species, one for balancing.
**Half equations** (1 mark each): put electrons on the correct side and check charge balances.
**Displacement observations** (2 marks): colour change of the solution, solid appearing on the metal, temperature rise.
**Why carbon cannot be used** (2 marks): the metal is more reactive than carbon, so it holds the oxygen more strongly.
**6-mark extended answer**: for extraction, name the ore, state the method, give equation, say which species is reduced and which is oxidised, and link to reactivity.
Use correct terms: 'oxidised' and 'reduced', not 'burnt' or 'reduced in size'.
Command word 'predict' for displacement: use the reactivity series; if the metal is lower than the one in solution, say no reaction.

mistakes.r: Oxidation is LOSS of electrons (OIL RIG). Gain of electrons is reduction.
The metal is oxidised (it gains oxygen / loses electrons). Oxygen is reduced because it gains electrons.
mistakes.w: The oxygen is oxidised when a metal burns.

mistakes.r: Oxidation and reduction always occur together; identify both the species oxidised and the species reduced.
mistakes.w: Only one substance is oxidised or reduced in a reaction.

mistakes.r: Sulfate ions are spectator ions and do not change. Cu2+ ions are reduced.
mistakes.w: The sulfate ions are reduced in Mg + CuSO4.

mistakes.r: Electrons are transferred: Mg → Mg2+ + 2e- and Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu. The electrons cancel in the overall equation.
mistakes.w: Mg + Cu2+ → Mg2+ + Cu has no electrons so it is not redox.

mistakes.r: Reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of electrons; mass changes are not part of the definition.
mistakes.w: Reduction means the substance gets smaller or lighter.

mistakes.r: Carbon only reduces oxides of metals less reactive than carbon; aluminium and above need electrolysis.
mistakes.w: Carbon can extract any metal from its oxide.

mistakes.r: Electrons are on the right in oxidation (lost) and on the left in reduction (gained).
mistakes.w: Electrons appear on the left of an oxidation half equation.

summary: AQA 4.4.1.3 expects you to define oxidation and reduction in terms of gain or loss of oxygen and (Higher tier) in terms of loss or gain of electrons, to identify which species is oxidised or reduced in a reaction, and to write ionic and half equations for displacement reactions and metals reacting with acids. It matters because reactivity, metal extraction, rusting, electrolysis, fuel cells and displacement all rely on electron transfer.

terms.d: Gain of oxygen by a substance.
Loss of oxygen from a substance.
Loss of electrons (Higher tier). Oxidation Is Loss.
Gain of electrons (Higher tier). Reduction Is Gain.
Memory aid: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction both take place.
A substance that causes another substance to be oxidised; it is itself reduced.
A substance that causes another substance to be reduced; it is itself oxidised.
A reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound.
An ion that is present in the reaction mixture but does not take part in the reaction and is unchanged.
An equation that shows only the particles that change, with spectator ions left out.
An equation showing either the oxidation or the reduction part of a reaction, including electrons.
A list of metals in order of how readily they react, i.e. how easily they lose electrons to form positive ions.
The negative electrode in electrolysis, where positive ions gain electrons (reduction).
The positive electrode in electrolysis, where negative ions lose electrons (oxidation).
A rock containing enough metal or metal compound to make it economic to extract the metal.

worked.ans: Mg + Cu2+ → Mg2+ + Cu. Magnesium is oxidised (Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-); copper ions are reduced (Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu).
worked.q: Magnesium is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. (a) Write the ionic equation. (b) Write half equations and state which species is oxidised and which is reduced. (4 marks)
steps: Symbol equation: Mg + CuSO4 → MgSO4 + Cu.
Spectator ion: SO4 2- is on both sides, so remove it.
Ionic equation: Mg + Cu2+ → Mg2+ + Cu (1 mark for species, 1 for balance).
Half equations: Mg → Mg2+ + 2e- (oxidation, loss of electrons); Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu (reduction, gain of electrons).

worked.ans: Model answer: Iron(III) oxide is reduced because it loses oxygen to form iron. Carbon monoxide is oxidised because it gains oxygen to form carbon dioxide.
worked.q: Iron(III) oxide is reduced in the blast furnace by carbon monoxide. Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2. Explain, using oxygen, which substance is reduced and which is oxidised. (3 marks)
steps: Iron(III) oxide changes to iron: it has lost oxygen, so it is reduced.
Carbon monoxide changes to carbon dioxide: it has gained oxygen, so it is oxidised.
Link: oxygen is transferred from the iron oxide to the carbon monoxide.

worked.ans: 56 tonnes of iron (check: 112/160 = 0.7 of the oxide mass, and 0.7 × 80 = 56).
worked.q: Calculate the mass of iron produced from 80 tonnes of pure iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3 (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16). (3 marks)
steps: Moles of Fe2O3 = 80 / 160 = 0.5 (units: tonne-moles, i.e. using tonnes with Mr).
From the equation 1 Fe2O3 gives 2 Fe, so Fe = 1.0 (same units). Mass of Fe = 1.0 × 56 = 56 tonnes.
